we have identified two retroviral vectors that provide high level expression of human ADA after gene transfer into hematopoietic human cell lines, and that the level of expression is maintained or increased during differentiation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of retroviral vectors that can provide optimal levels of gene expression in human bone marrow cells.

the identification of vectors that provide optimal expression of a therapeutic gene in the hematopoietic stem cell, and with the identification of conditions that maximize the therapeutic effect of gene transfer into these cells.
the identification and characterization of the optimal retroviral vectors for the transfer of the ADA gene to human hematopoietically derived cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LASN and LNCG vectors are superior to all other vectors tested for the introduction of a therapeutic gene into the bone marrow of patients with ADA deficiency.
the LASN and LNCGA vectors are superior for ADA gene transfer into human marrow cells.
the ADA gene is transcribed from the strong promoters of LASN and LNCE vectors, which provide optimal gene expression and may be useful for gene therapy of ADA-deficient patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ADA gene is expressed in hematopoietic and non-hematopoietic cells under the control of a strong viral promoter, but that the ADA gene may be expressed more efficiently in differentiating hematopoieitic cells.
LASN and LNCE are the best ADA expression vectors in hematopoietic stem cells.
the ADA gene can be expressed in hematopoietic progenitor cells at high levels from vectors containing strong promoters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ADA expression from the LASN and LN CA vectors in hematopoietic progenitors is sufficient to correct ADA-deficient cells in vitro.
the LASN and LN CA vectors provide high levels of ADA expression and are suitable for gene therapy of ADA deficiency.
the ADA gene under transcriptional control of a strong promoter/enhancer is expressed at levels that should be sufficient for gene therapy.
